constitutive_assumptions: Planar sensing coils are attached to rigid internal fins, assuming the coil plane remains in quadrature with the inner tangent of the finger during bending.
The inner periphery (grasping area) length remains constant during bending, while the outer periphery expands.
Relative movement at the bottom edges of the coils (<0.5 mm) has a negligible effect on mutual inductance compared to the angular displacement at the outer edges (5 mm).
Operating below the self-resonance frequency (200 kHz) at 50 kHz ensures inductive coil impedance dominates and parasitic capacitance effects are negligible.
Constant current excitation prevents changes in coil contact resistance or ambient temperature from altering primary excitation current.
Small DC offsets and op-amp bias currents do not induce secondary AC voltages.
control_variables: Excitation frequency (50 kHz) and voltage (1 V p-p)
Primary coil excitation current (1.6 mA) set via 220 Ohm input resistor
Planar coil geometry (16 mm x 16 mm PCB, 26 turns, 0.127 mm trace width/spacing, 0.035 mm copper thickness, 0.3 mm substrate thickness)
Initial coil spacing in relaxed state (~5 mm)
Gripper finger dimensions (11.5 cm length, 2.5 cm width, 5.5 cm finger-to-finger distance)
Silicone elastomer material (Smooth-On Dragon Skin 20 Platinum cure silicone) and PLA structural fins
dependent_variables: Secondary coil induced voltage (Vp-p or Voi)
Mutual inductance between coil pairs (M1, M2, M3)
Segment bend angles (theta_1, theta_2, theta_3 for tip, middle, and base segments)
Polynomial calibration coefficients (k0, k1, k2) and goodness-of-fit (R^2)

evidence_relevant_to_topic.claim: Mutual inductance between flexible planar coil pairs attached to internal rigid fins decreases monotonically as bend angle increases from 0 to 120 degrees due to increasing upper-edge separation.

Segmented bend angle sensing using three independent coil pairs across base, middle, and tip regions successfully distinguishes grasp modes (pinch vs. enveloping) and object shapes (spherical vs. rectangular).

The magnetic coupling bend sensor achieved an average sensitivity of 1.05 mV/deg with a second-order polynomial fit R^2 of 0.999 over 0 to 120 degrees, with repeatability within 0.5 degrees (0.11 mV standard deviation).
A series-connected current source excitation scheme eliminates measurement sensitivity to contact resistance variations and ambient temperature fluctuations.
Grasping ferromagnetic objects (relative permeability 1200) and conductive copper objects caused negligible interference in mutual inductance due to spatial separation (8 mm) and localized core flux.
Optical validation using CAD image analysis verified dynamic bend angle tracking with errors ranging from 0.1 to 0.9 degrees relative to visual ground truth.

experimental_setup: Pneumatically actuated two-finger soft robotic gripper fabricated by casting Smooth-On Dragon Skin 20 silicone onto a 3D-printed PLA mold with internal PLA rigid fins (finger dimensions: 11.5 cm x 2.5 cm; limb spacing: 5.5 cm).
Six identical planar spiral coil flexible PCBs (16 mm x 16 mm x 0.3 mm, 26 turns, 4.95 uH self-inductance) mounted on internal rigid fins forming three sensor pairs (tip, middle, base).
Current source driver using an LF347 quad JFET op-amp supplying 1.6 mA AC current at 50 kHz across series-connected primary coils.
Signal conditioning unit with AD620 instrumentation amplifiers (gain = 100) and bandpass filtering.
National Instruments NI ELVIS II+ DAQ unit running custom LabVIEW software sampling at 500 kHz.
Static calibration jig with precision grooves from 0 to 120 degrees in 20-degree increments.
CAD-based optical angle verification using camera recordings and Autodesk Inventor.
Grasping test rig evaluating pinch and enveloping grasps on spherical, rectangular, ferromagnetic (steel tube, relative permeability 1200), and conductive (copper) targets.
future_work: Using the combined multi-segment bend angle outputs to automate recognition and classification of object shapes.
Implementing synchronous demodulation signal processing and dynamic excitation frequency switching to mitigate external time-varying magnetic interference.
independent_variables: Bend angle of the soft robotic finger segment (0 to 120 degrees in 20-degree increments; dynamic cyclic bending)
Primary excitation AC frequency (50 kHz) and voltage (1 V p-p)
Grasping modality (enveloping grasp vs. pinch grasp)
Object geometry/shape (spherical balls, square/rectangular blocks, varying diameters)
Object material electromagnetic properties (ferromagnetic with relative permeability 1200, conductive copper)
limitations_inferred: The sensor architecture requires pre-existing internal rigid fins or skeleton structures for mounting, making it difficult to implement in finless, entirely elastomeric, or hollow soft actuators without structural modifications.
Sensing is restricted to single-axis planar bending; out-of-plane lateral deflection, torsional twisting, or elongation are not measured or decoupled.
The sensor provides proprioceptive curvature information only and cannot measure contact forces or grasp pressure.
Object shape identification is currently qualitative based on discrete segment angles; no automated classification algorithm was implemented or demonstrated.
Long-term cyclic fatigue of PCB traces, bonding durability to PLA fins, and lead-wire fatigue under extended cycles were not evaluated.
limitations_stated_by_authors: Misalignment of PCBs in the relaxed position and non-uniform periphery expansion from fabrication defects cause minor parameter variations across individual sensor calibration curves.
Anatomical irregularities in finger design (unequal slice counts per segment replicating human finger anatomy) prevent the finger from being segmented into equal geometric thirds.
Susceptibility to interference if exposed to external time-varying magnetic fields operating near the excitation frequency.
Coil turn count and maximum mutual inductance are limited by PCB manufacturing constraints on minimum trace width and trace gap.
PCB physical dimensions must not exceed the internal rigid fin profile (15 mm x 15 mm or 16 mm x 16 mm) and must remain very thin to avoid restricting finger flexibility.
main_results: Demonstrated monotonic decrease in mutual inductance and secondary induced voltage as bend angle increases from 0 to 120 degrees, matching finite element simulation results.
Established high measurement linearity to a second-order polynomial calibration curve with R^2 = 0.999 and average sensitivity of 1.05 mV/deg.

Achieved high repeatability across cyclic actuation with a maximum standard deviation of 0.11 mV (corresponding to 0.5 degrees at maximum bend angle) and agreement within 0.1 to 0.9 degrees of CAD image references.

Successfully distinguished object geometry and grasp modes: spherical objects yielded near-equal tip and middle angles (theta_1 ~= theta_2), rectangular objects yielded distinct segment angles, and pinch grasps produced higher overall bend angles than enveloping grasps.
Demonstrated immunity to conductive and ferromagnetic objects placed in the grasp region (8 mm separation), exhibiting negligible interference on mutual inductance measurements.
modeling_methods: Finite element analysis (FEA) using the AC/DC magnetic field (mf) module in COMSOL Multiphysics software to model mutual inductance versus bend angle from 0 to 50 degrees.
Analytical formula calculating mutual inductance from secondary induced voltage: M = Vs / (omega * Ip).
Second-order polynomial empirical regression curve fitting: Voi = k2*theta^2 - k1*theta + k0.
Analytical transfer relationship for instrumentation amplifier output: Voi = (omega * Vs * G / R1) * Mi.
CAD-based geometric angle extraction using Autodesk Inventor on digital camera images of the bending actuator.
performance_metrics: Bend angle measurement range: 0 to 120 degrees
Output repeatability / standard deviation: maximum SD of 0.0023 V (calibration) and 0.11 mV (dynamic cycling, corresponding to 0.5 degrees at maximum bend angle)
Optical CAD reference comparison absolute error: 0.1 to 0.9 degrees
Planar coil coupling coefficient: 0.1 (parallel, unbent configuration)
possible_gap_implications: Integrating localized non-contact inductive bend angle sensing into soft pneumatic fingers provides proprioceptive feedback immune to resistive hysteresis and capacitive environmental drift, potentially enabling closed-loop shape-adaptive grasping and object recognition. However, adapting this approach to general soft continuum robots requires overcoming reliance on rigid internal mounting fins, addressing multi-axis bending and twisting, and developing automated shape reconstruction algorithms.
paper.research_objective: To design, fabricate, and experimentally evaluate a flexible planar-coil-based segmented bend angle sensor integrated into the internal fins of a soft robotic gripper, using series current-source excitation to accurately measure local bend angles up to 120 degrees and provide object shape feedback during grasping.
paper.research_problem: Exact dynamic modeling and control of soft robotic grippers are challenging due to non-linear material properties, and existing bend angle sensors (resistive, capacitive, optical) suffer from hysteresis, environmental susceptibility (humidity, dust, temperature), high power/cost, or measure only overall structure displacement rather than segmented, localized bend angles necessary to identify non-circular object shapes.
paper.title: Design and Implementation of a Magnetic Coupling Based Segmented Bend Angle Sensor for a Soft Robotic Gripper
